title: Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum

{{Short description|Species of cactus}} {{Speciesbox |image = Teguise Guatiza - Jardin - Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum 02 ies.jpg |status = LC |status_system = IUCN3.1 |status_ref ={{cite journal | title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species | journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species | date=2009-04-29 | url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en | access-date=2023-08-13 | page=}} |genus = Pachycereus |species = pecten-aboriginum | authority = [[Nathaniel Lord Britton|Britton]] & [[Joseph Nelson Rose|Rose]]Under its accepted name of ''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum'' (from its basionym, ''Cereus pecten-aboriginum'') this species was published in ''Contributions from the United States National Herbarium'' 12(10): 422. 1909. {{ cite web |url=http://tropicos.org/Name/50003419 |title=Name - ''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum'' Britton & Rose. |work=Tropicos |publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |location=[[Saint Louis, Missouri]] |accessdate=April 30, 2012}} |synonyms = *''Cereus pecten-aboriginum''
[[George Engelmann|Engelm.]] ex [[Sereno Watson|S.Watson]] ([[basionym]]) |synonyms_ref = The basionym of ''P. pecten-aboriginum'' (''Cereus pecten-aboriginum'') was originally described and published in ''Proceedings of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences'' 21: 429–430. 1886. {{ cite web |url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/5103786 |title=Name - ''Cereus pecten-aboriginum'' Engelm. ex S.Watson |work=Tropicos |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |location=Saint Louis, Missouri |accessdate=April 30, 2012}} }} '''''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum''''' (commonly known as '''hairbrush''' or '''Indian comb''') is a columnar [[cactus]] plant native to [[Mexico]]. They can grow up to {{cvt|15|m|abbr=on}} high. The trunk of this species is 1.2 to 5.0 m tall and the fruits are large and burr-like. The specific name, ''pecten-aboriginum'', is from the [[Latin]], and means "native combs". It was inspired by the use of the fruits as [[comb|hair combs]].{{cite book |author=Shreve, S. and I. L. Wiggins |title=Vegetation and Flora of the Sonoran Desert |url=https://archive.org/details/vegetationflorao0001shre |url-access=registration |publisher=[[Stanford University Press]] |location=Stanford, CA |year=1964}} ==Description== ''P. pecten-aboriginum'' is a tree up to 15 m tall with many branches. The erect or ascending branches are up to {{cvt|25|cm|abbr=on}} in diameter. Trunks of up to 2 meters in diameter are formed. The deep green, immature stems are up to 22 cm wide with 10 or 11 ribs. Mature stems are up to 17.5 cm wide with 10 to 12 ribs that are slightly rounded. They have a diameter of {{cvt|9 to 13|cm}}. The [[areole]]s bear rigid, sharp, white to gray spines, that are up to {{cvt|1 to 3|cm}} long which may be curved on mature stems.{{ cite book |author=Turner, R. M.|title=Sonoran Desert Plants: An Ecological Atlas. |publisher=[[University of Arizona Press]] |location=[[University of Arizona]], Tucson, AZ |year=2005|display-authors=etal}} The eight to nine radial spines are up to {{cvt|1|cm}} and greyish. The flower is white and about 5.0 to 7.5 cm long. It opens in the evening and closes by midday. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is coated in velvety brown hairs. The floral [[bract]]s are linear with long-attenuated tips covering the development of flower buds. Flowering occurs January through March. The fruit is densely covered with long, golden yellow spines up to 6 cm long. It ripens by June and July. It [[Dehiscence (botany)|splits]] at maturity to reveal a thin layer of firm, red, juicy pulp and shiny black seeds, each about 0.5 cm long.{{cite book | last1=Anderson | first1=Edward F. | last2=Eggli | first2=Urs | title=Das grosse Kakteen-Lexikon | date=2005 | isbn=3-8001-4573-1 | language=de | page=492| publisher=Ulmer }} File:Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum (5769162340).jpg|Adult plant File:Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum (24011869590).jpg|Flowers File:Pachycereus pectin-aboriginum (26846018022).jpg|Fruits File:Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum 2019-12-13 6498.jpg|Spines File:Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum 0zz.jpg|Growth ==Distribution== ''P. pecten-aboriginum'' is [[endemism|endemic]] to Mexico.Arreola, H., et al. 2013. [http://www.iucnredlist.org/details/152790/0 ''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum''.] In: IUCN 2013. IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Version 2013.1. Downloaded on 26 August 2013. Its range extends throughout the western states from [[Baja California]] through [[Sinaloa]] and [[Sonora]] to [[Chiapas]]. It grows in the [[Chihuahuan Desert|Chihuahuan]] and [[Sonoran Desert]]s, the [[thorn forest]] of [[Sinaloa]], and the southern Sonoran plains. ===Habitat=== ''P. pecten-aboriginum'' is found on slopes and plains, and in valleys and [[Arroyo (watercourse)|arroyo]]s. Its habitat includes thorn scrubs, tropical deciduous forests, and Sonoran desert scrub.{{ cite book |last=Felger | first = R. S.|title=The Trees of Sonora, Mexico |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |location=Oxford, UK |year=2001|display-authors=etal}} It grows on flat land and hills and in canyons.{{ cite book |author=Britton, N. L. and J. N. Rose |title=The Cactaceae |volume=2 |publisher=[[Carnegie Institution of Washington]] |location=Washington, D.C| year=1920}} It is abundant in the [[subtropics|subtropical]] scrub of southern [[Sonora]], particularly in the foothills and lower mountains. ===Biology=== ''P. pecten-aboriginum'' is a [[Ploidy#Diploid|diploid]] plant. Its floral biology differs across its range. In [[Tehuacán, Puebla|Tehuacán]], it is [[pollination|pollinated]] at night by [[nectar]]-feeding [[bat]]s. In the Sonoran desert, the flowers stay open longer in the day to attract both nocturnal and diurnal pollinators.{{ cite journal |url=http://ac.els-cdn.com/S0140196302003233/1-s2.0-S0140196302003233-main.pdf?_tid=757c441a5936d7458a5f3e7914b13d8b&acdnat=1335759747_606d882a929829a51c6ba14824985bd7 |journal=Journal of Arid Environments |volume=56 |issue=1 |date=January 2004 |pages=117–127 |title=Pollination biology of the columnar cactus ''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum'' in north-western México |author=Molina-Freaner, F.|doi=10.1016/s0140-1963(02)00323-3|display-authors=etal}} ==Taxonomy== The plant was first described as ''Cereus pecten-aboriginum'' 1886 by [[Sereno Watson]].{{cite book | last=Arts | first=American Academy of | title=Proceedings of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences | publisher=Metcalf and Co | volume=v. 21, new ser. v. 13 (1885-1886) | date=1885 | issn=0199-9818 | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/8865363#page/455/mode/1up | access-date=2023-08-13}} [[Nathaniel Lord Britton]] and [[Joseph Nelson Rose]] placed them in the genus ''[[Pachycereus]]'' in 1909.{{cite web | last=States. | first=United | title=Contributions from the United States National Herbarium | publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press | volume=v.12 (1908-1909) | date=1908 | url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/367832#page/551/mode/1up | access-date=2023-08-13}} ==Uses== ===Food=== The fruit can be eaten raw or cooked, and can be made into a [[syrup]] or [[fruit preserves|preserves]] or jam. It has been used to make [[wine]]. The [[Mayo people]] made [[tortilla]]s from the ground seeds mixed with some [[corn meal]]. This so-called etcho-seed flour was used in [[breakfast]] foods such as [[pancake]]s. ===Medicinal=== The Mayo used the cactus as an herbal remedy. Pieces of the flesh were applied to wounds to inhibit [[bleeding]]. The cactus flesh was cooked in salted water and the solution was applied to infected wounds three times daily, followed by a [[sulfathiazole]] powder. The juice was consumed as an [[herbal tonic]] and to treat [[sore throat]].{{ cite book |author=Kay, M. A. |title=Healing with Plants in the American and Mexican West |publisher=University of Arizona Press |location=University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ |year=1996}} ===Psychoactive=== The cactus has been used by the [[Tarahuma people]] to produce [[narcotic]] effects.{{cite journal | last1=Schultes | first1=Richard Evans | last2=Farnsworth | first2=Norman R | title=Ethnomedical, Botanical and Phytochemical Aspects of Natural Hallucinogens | journal=Botanical Museum leaflets, Harvard University | volume=28 | issue=2 | date=1980 | issn=0006-8098 | doi=10.5962/p.168645 | pages=123–214 | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41762829 | access-date=17 July 2026}} It is known to contain [[carnegine]]. ===Grooming=== The fruits were used as combs by indigenous peoples. To make a [[hairbrush]], the spines were removed from about two-thirds of the fruit, and the remaining spines were trimmed to about 1 cm in length. == References == {{Reflist|2}} ==External links== *{{Commons category-inline|Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum|''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum''}} *{{Wikispecies-inline|Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum|''Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum''}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q150206}} [[Category:Pachycereus]] [[Category:Plants described in 1886]] [[Category:Endemic flora of Mexico]]
